young.html: Fifty years after the Greeks beat the Persians, the two strongest Greek cities went to war with each other: Athens, a democracy with a great navy and an empire of island allies, and Sparta, a city of soldiers with the best army in Greece and its own league of allies. The war lasted 27 years, from 431 to 404 BC, and Sparta won.

An Athenian named Thucydides wrote its history. He was there: he caught the terrible plague that struck Athens, and he commanded ships in the war. When he failed to save a city from the Spartans, the Athenians sent him away, and he spent twenty years in exile, which gave him time to talk to people on both sides.

Thucydides wanted to get things exactly right. He didn't put in stories about gods or monsters. He checked what people told him, because, he said, eyewitnesses often remember the same event differently. He hoped his book would be useful long after his own time, to anyone who wanted to understand how wars start and what they do to people.

young.html: Two eyewitnesses. Have two people watch the same short scene (a pet, the street outside, a minute of a ball game), then each write down, without talking, exactly what happened. Compare. What did both notice? What did only one see? Thucydides said that is why a historian must check every account.

full.text: A history written from inside the war

Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, beginning at the moment that it broke out, and believing that it would be a great war, and more worthy of relation than any that had preceded it.
full.author: Thucydides
full.work: History of the Peloponnesian War, Book I
full.ed: J. M. Dent and Sons (Everyman's Library)

full.html: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC) was a wealthy Athenian with family ties to Thrace. He survived the plague of 430 BC and was elected a general in 424 BC; when the Spartan commander Brasidas took the city of Amphipolis before he could arrive, he was exiled for twenty years. His history, later divided into eight books, breaks off in 411 BC, seven years before the war ended. The historian Xenophon carried the story on.

Method. In Book I, Thucydides explains that he checked reports of events as carefully as he could, because witnesses disagree and memory is partial. For speeches, he says, he gives what each speaker most likely said, keeping as close as he could to the general sense. He hopes his work will be "a possession for all time", useful because human nature makes such things happen again.
He also separates the stated quarrels that set off the war from what he calls its truest cause: the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta.

full.html: At the public funeral after the first year of war, the Athenian leader Pericles praised not the dead men one by one but the city they died for: a democracy, he said, where power rests with the many, where people are judged by merit, where citizens take part in public affairs and the city is open to the world, "the school of Hellas". It is one of the most famous speeches in history, and also, as Thucydides shows by what comes next, an ideal: the plague strikes Athens the very next summer.
In 416 BC Athens demanded that the small neutral island of Melos join its empire. Thucydides writes the negotiation as a dialogue. The Melians appeal to justice and the gods. The Athenians answer:

full.text: … since you know as well as we do that right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
full.author: Thucydides
full.work: History of the Peloponnesian War, Book V
full.ed: J. M. Dent and Sons (Everyman's Library)
full.note: The end of a sentence. The speakers are the Athenian envoys; Thucydides does not say he agrees with them.

full.html: Melos refused, was besieged and fell; the Athenians put the men to death and enslaved the women and children. In the next book, Athens sets out with great confidence to conquer Sicily, and loses its fleet and army.

Thucydides does not tell the reader what to think. He sets speeches side by side (Pericles and the Spartan king Archidamus; Cleon and Diodotus on Mytilene; the Athenians and the Melians) and lets events answer them. Readers have argued ever since about what his own view was.
Treating the speeches as word-for-word records. Thucydides says plainly that they are his reconstructions of what was said, or of what the occasion called for.

deep.html: Describing civil strife at Corcyra in 427 BC, Thucydides says that war is a violent teacher: in hard times, people's tempers sink to their circumstances, and even the meanings of words change, so that reckless daring is called loyal courage and caution is called cowardice. He gives the plague the same cool attention, describing its symptoms so that it could be recognized if it ever came again.

The book describes the plague, massacres and the fate of the defeated, plainly and without sensation. Parents may want to preview Books II (the plague), III (Corcyra), V (Melos) and VII (the end in Sicily). For young readers, the Funeral Oration and the story of the Sicilian Expedition read aloud work well.

items: Is it true that the strong do what they can? Should it be? Who in the history seems to think otherwise?
What is the difference between a stated reason for a war and its real cause?
Can a democracy run an empire and stay a democracy?
Is history useful for the future, as Thucydides hoped, or does every age face new problems?

deep.html: Thomas Hobbes, later on this ladder, made the first English translation directly from the Greek (1629) and said Thucydides taught him how dangerous democracy could be. Others have read him as the great defender of Athenian freedom. Plato's Republic and Aristotle's Politics, on the next rungs, take up the same questions of justice and power in philosophy.

questions: Thucydides said eyewitnesses remember the same event differently. Why do you think that happens?
Pericles said Athens was a "school" for the rest of Greece. What would you want your town or country to teach others?
The Athenians told the Melians that the strong do what they can. Do you agree? What could the Melians have said back?
Thucydides wanted his book to be useful forever. What lesson from history do you think everyone should know?
He was exiled for failing at his job, and then he became one of the greatest historians. What good can come out of a failure?
care: The history describes the plague of Athens, massacres and the fate of captured cities, plainly. This lesson summarizes them without detail. Young readers can start with the Funeral Oration and the story of the Sicilian Expedition, read with a parent.
